chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Dawud ibn al-Nu'man and Saif ibn 'Amirah, from Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'A man does not have anything of the fitrah (alms of fasting) except what he pays for himself alone; he gives it for a stranger, or he eats it himself and his dependents.' He said: 'He gives to some of his dependents, then the other gives for himself; they alternate it, so it becomes one fitrah for all of them.'

key_terms.الْفِطْرَة: Zakat al-Fitr, the alms tax paid at the end of Ramadan
key_terms.عِيَالُهُ: His dependents (family members supported by him)
key_terms.فِطْرَةٌ وَاحِدَةٌ: One fitrah (collective fulfillment of the obligation)
key_terms.يُرَدِّدُونَهَا: They alternate it (rotating the payment obligation)

ai.seo_question: How should a family distribute Zakat al-Fitr if they have limited funds?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the flexibility in fulfilling Zakat al-Fitr for a family with limited means, permitting the obligation to be shared or rotated among members rather than requiring individual payment for each dependent. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle of easing financial burdens (*rukhas*) while maintaining the communal spirit of purification. It underscores the practical application of *fitrah* as a collective household duty when resources are scarce, ensuring no member is left without the spiritual cleansing associated with the end of Ramadan.
